# **Platinum supply issues** 

_The potential impact of safety stoppages, electricity supply, high costs, low prices and strikes on pgm output._ 

#### **David Jollie** 

**david.jollie@mitprecious.com Tel: +44 20 7489 6767** 

#### **03 February 2012** 

#### **New York:** 

- Supply side issues have recently come to the fore for platinum once again in the form of concerns over electricity supply, safety stoppages and industrial action. 

- Although none of the recent issues (safety stoppages, electricity supply, a tense labour relations climate and high and rising production costs) should be a surprise to the market, they have the potential to depress South African platinum group metal output this year. They are also likely to contribute to longer term cost pressures, supporting platinum prices in particular over a multi-year timescale due to the geographical concentration of platinum mining in South Africa. 

• Our models of the platinum group metal markets suggest that platinum is in a small surplus this year while palladium is set to be in a deficit. We therefore feel that there is potential for supply side issues to drive the prices of platinum and palladium higher in the shorter term. We believe that the surplus in the rhodium market is sufficiently large that any positive price impact from supply disruption should be rather limited.

## **<mark>Platinum production</mark>** 

Supply side issues have recently come to the fore for platinum again in the form of concerns over electricity supply, safety stoppages and industrial action. While none of these issues should be a particular surprise to the market, they all illustrate the upside risk to the platinum price in the short and long terms due to the geographical concentration of platinum mining in South Africa. 

## **<mark>Electricity supply</mark>** 

The first supply side issue to hit the headlines this year was concern over the short term availability of electricity from Eskom, the South African electricity provider. As is widely known, the subsidisation of electricity costs by the South African government over a period of many years left Eskom with insufficient funds to invest to build capacity and maintain equipment fully. With the South African economy having expanded in recent years and electricity generating capacity constrained, the margin of spare capacity has progressively been reduced. 

This situation came to a head in January 2008. Increas

ingly frequent interruptions to electricity supplies (euphemistically-termed “load shedding”) made it unsafe to operate underground mining or even the smelting process, disrupting pgm production and sending metal prices higher. Quick remedial action to reduce energy usage restored some of the spare capacity and led to a more stable electricity supply. However, continued economic growth has once again reduced the margin of excess electricity generating capacity since then. 

The southern hemisphere summer sees high levels of power use in South Africa (including for air conditioning) and also sees substantial amounts of maintenance being carried out on the power generation infrastructure. The margin between available power and electricity requirements can often shrink at this time of year, so news stories addressing this issue should not be a surprise.  Comments from Eskom this week calling on South Africans to reduce their electricity usage simply reinforce the sense that continuous electricity supply cannot entirely be relied upon. The question is, however, whether they indicate a potential short term disruption to platinum mining and refining. 

We do not expect metal production within South Africa to be affected negatively by this issue in the very short term. Although it is impossible to ignore the chance of significant electricity supply problems developing, there currently seems to be sufficient power generation to meet demand. Additionally, following the crisis in 2008, the mining industry installed more back-up power and also reduced the amount of electricity it uses somewhat. This means that production should be more robust, even if some power outages occur, with minor supply problems unlikely to cause major disruption to mining, smelting or refining. 

To improve transparency, Eskom is now issuing very regular updates of expected electricity demand and available generating capacity. The table below indicates the expected operational deficit for each week until mid-April, excluding operational reserves and unplanned outages of  a combined 6,400 MW, and shows that demand is forecast to be above Eskom’s comfort zone for most of the next few months. 

Without further demand side measures, generating capacity is not expected to meet consumer demand by roughly mid-April. If unplanned outages also occur, this crunch could occur sooner. However, we note that consumer action can be expected to reduce overall electricity demand somewhat (which is why Eskom is calling for energy saving from its customers). Nonetheless, we caution that there is some possibility of disruption and that the _risks_ to the platinum and palladium prices are only upwards. In timing terms, the market seems most prone to this disruption during April and May.

er the longer term, the picture is more complex. Several large new power plants are being constructed and this should restore the safety margin by 2016. However, if the South African economy continues to grow as expected, then there will continue to be constraints on electricity supply. New mining operations may face challenges or delays in securing electricity supplies from Eskom. This should not prevent the construction of new mines but it will add to long run cost pressures, providing a further degree of support for platinum prices. 

## **<mark>Safety stoppages</mark>** 

Section 54 has become a much more commonly-heard phrase across the platinum mining sector in recent months. Section 54 of the Mine Health and Safety Amendment Act 2008 results in a compulsory shutdown of mining operations to enable investigation into the cause of fatal incidents. The Department of Mineral Resources can also use Section 54 notices to shut down a shaft deemed unsafe before an incident occurs. 

Over recent years, the average length of time mining is suspended by a Section 54 notice has risen sharply. Additionally, such stoppages have increased dramatically in frequency, particularly in the Rustenburg area where the bulk of platinum mining takes place. For example, Anglo American Platinum recently reported 81 safety stoppages in calendar year 2011 compared with 36 a year earlier. Indeed the number of stoppages at its operations was almost as high in Q4 2011 as in the whole of 2010. Other miners including Impala, Lonmin and Aquarius have also pointed to the greatly increased frequency of safety stoppages in their financial results as a contributory factor in rising costs and lowerthan-planned mine output. 

Given the focus on zero fatalities and zero harm by regulators and the mining industry itself, it seems unlikely that the safety regime will be significantly loosened in terms of the number of safety stoppages enforced. However, recent comments by South Africa’s chief mine inspector did reveal an emphasis on reducing the amount of production lost per stoppage. Both Amplats and Lonmin have reported that they are in discussions with the Ministry on ways to improve the situation. We are moderately optimistic that some reduction in lost production can be achieved without any negative impact upon mine safety as a result of these discussions. 

Section 54 and other safety issues will remain a real concern for the industry. However, they are unlikely to lead to a major fall in metal output. Their increasing frequency and

lengthening duration do, though, pose a threat to the maximum level of production from any particular mine and impose an additional cost on platinum mining. In the short term, this safety regime poses a formidable barrier to expanding platinum output significantly. In the longer term, it is an additional cost which will require a mining house to have greater

face availability at its operations in order to achieve the same output, resulting in lower profitability or higher prices. 

## **<mark>Strikes</mark>** 

Last year we commented on the round of wage negotiations due to take place in the South African platinum mining industry. Although negotiations were drawn out and wage increases were some way above the level of domestic inflation, there was surprisingly little industrial action (essentially strike activity) directly related to the wage negotiations. There were however, a number of strikes throughout the industry last year over a range of issues from wages to union recognition to safety and so on, with an associated negative impact on platinum group metal production. 

Most of the platinum producers agreed two year above inflation deals last year, so the most frequent cause of industrial action - wage disputes - is likely to be less of an issue than it was last year. However, the industrial relations climate within South Africa remains somewhat heated. At Impala, for instance, an illegal strike broke out on the 20<sup>th</sup> of January 2012 and was still continuing in early February. Losses were estimated at a little under 3,000 ounces of platinum group metals per day (although the processing of above ground stocks means that real losses of refined output will be deferred and could well be lower). 

We expect to see further strikes sporadically during 2012 (although, clearly, we cannot accurately forecast either their cause or duration) and expect this to restrain any growth in platinum output from South Africa to low levels at best this year. 

## **<mark>Production costs/low prices</mark>** 

The impact of a high cost of production as a source of support for platinum prices has been widely discussed. We do not propose to cover this issue in detail in this report. However, we note that the producers are not oblivious to this issue. Last year, Impala “rightsized” its Marula operations in response to underperformance. Recently, Aquarius announced plans to review operations at its Everest property, and it intends to maintain production below maximum capacity whilst this review is carried out. 

Although relatively few cuts in mine production have been made so far due to high costs or low profitability, sustained low prices can only have a further negative impact on platinum group metal output. 

## **<mark>Overall impact</mark>** 

Our fundamental view of the platinum group metal markets is that platinum itself should be in a small surplus this year, while palladium should be in deficit. Rhodium is in a more substantial surplus. 

Outside South Africa, production is unlikely to rise significantly this year. In Zimbabwe, Zimplats and Mimosa are operating at steady state. Unki reached steady state only in Q4 2011 and Zimbabwe will therefore produce more metal this year than last year. However, Norilsk Nickel recently revealed more negative production plans for 2012. Nickel output from the company

’s Russian operations is expected to fall and palladium production is forecast to decline from 2.81 million ounces to 2.6-2.65 million ounces. Refined platinum output is expected to drop from 695,000 ounces to 650-660,000 ounces.

Safety and the other issues discussed above mean that South African pgm production itself will struggle to climb from last year’s levels. As importantly, there is a reasonable chance that production could fall due to one, or a combination, of these factors. We therefore feel that there is potential for supply side issues to drive the prices of platinum and palladium higher. We believe that the surplus in the rhodium market is sufficiently large that any positive price impact from supply disruption should be rather limited.
